title: Classification Metrics
html:
Every classification metric is built from the four cells of the confusion matrix. Pick the one that reflects what errors cost in your problem — accuracy alone is rarely enough.

The confusion matrix

Predicted positivePredicted negative
Actual positiveTrue positive (TP)False negative (FN) — Type II error, a miss
Actual negativeFalse positive (FP) — Type I error, a false alarmTrue negative (TN)
Watch out

scikit-learn orders labels ascending, so for 0/1 labels the matrix is [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]] — negatives first, the opposite of most textbook diagrams. Unpack with tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel().

The metrics

MetricFormulaQuestion it answers
Accuracy(TP + TN) / allWhat fraction of predictions are right?
PrecisionTP / (TP + FP)When the model says positive, how often is it right?
Recall (sensitivity, TPR)TP / (TP + FN)What fraction of actual positives does it find?
Specificity (TNR)TN / (TN + FP)What fraction of actual negatives does it clear?
False positive rateFP / (FP + TN) = 1 − specificityHow many negatives get a false alarm?
F12·P·R / (P + R)Harmonic mean of precision and recall
Fβ(1 + β²)·P·R / (β²·P + R)β > 1 weights recall more; β < 1 precision
Balanced accuracy(TPR + TNR) / 2Accuracy that isn't fooled by imbalance
MCC(TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN))Correlation between prediction and truth, −1 … 1
Log-loss−mean[y·log p + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)]How good are the predicted probabilities?
Key point

Precision and recall pull against each other: raising the decision threshold usually increases precision and lowers recall. F1 is high only when both are high — the harmonic mean is dragged toward the smaller one.

The accuracy paradox

Multi-class: averaging

AverageHowUse when
MacroCompute the metric per class, then the plain meanEvery class matters equally (rare classes count as much as common ones)
WeightedPer-class metric weighted by class supportSummarise overall performance, respecting class sizes
MicroPool all TP/FP/FN, then computeOverall per-prediction performance; for single-label multi-class, micro-F1 = accuracy

The rare class “bird” is never predicted: macro-F1 exposes that, while accuracy and micro-F1 (both 0.7) hide it.

Which metric?

SituationPrefer
Balanced classes, equal error costsAccuracy (plus the confusion matrix)
False positives are expensive (spam filter, a costly intervention)Precision (at a minimum recall)
False negatives are expensive (disease screening, fraud)Recall (at a minimum precision), F2
Imbalanced, need one threshold-free numberPR-AUC (average precision); also MCC at a chosen threshold
Ranking quality, roughly balancedROC-AUC
Probabilities will be used as probabilitiesLog-loss, Brier score, calibration curve
Real costs knownExpected cost / profit at the chosen threshold
Explain precision and recall with an example.

A fraud model flags 100 transactions; 80 are really fraud → precision 0.8. There were 200 frauds in total; it caught 80 → recall 0.4. Precision is about the trustworthiness of alarms, recall about coverage of the positives.

When is F1 a poor choice?

When error costs are very asymmetric (use Fβ or expected cost), when true negatives matter (F1 ignores them), when you care about probabilities rather than a single threshold, and when the positive class is not the one of interest — F1 depends on which class is labelled positive.

What is the difference between macro and micro averaging?

Macro averages the per-class scores, so each class counts equally and poor performance on a rare class shows up. Micro pools all decisions before computing, so frequent classes dominate; for single-label multi-class problems micro-precision, micro-recall and micro-F1 all equal accuracy.
